turns.content: I'm looking at the draft write-up I typed up for Mateo. I'll read it to you: "Employee failed to provide timely notice of absence. Mateo was scheduled Wednesday 5-10pm and did not notify management of inability to work until 3:30pm day-of, in violation of the 24-hour advance notice policy." Does that sound right to file tomorrow morning? Because I'm still standing here at the prize counter running both stations solo tonight and I'm pretty hot about it. But Clara's the one who made the schedule.

I’d **hold off on filing it as a confirmed policy violation** until you check the scheduling details with Clara. Running both stations solo is frustrating, but the write-up needs to separate what happened from who was responsible.

The key questions are:
- **When was the schedule posted or communicated to Mateo?** Was the shift added or changed within that 24-hour window?
- **When did Mateo learn he couldn’t work, and what reason did he give?** An unexpected illness or emergency may need different handling under policy or applicable leave rules.
- **Does the 24-hour rule apply in these circumstances?**

Your draft establishes that he gave **90 minutes’ notice**, but “failed” and “in violation” are conclusions you haven’t necessarily established yet.

For now, a neutral incident note would be:

> “Mateo was listed on the schedule for Wednesday, [date], from 5:00–10:00 p.m. At 3:30 p.m. that day, he notified [manager/name] that he was unable to work the shift. Schedule communication and the circumstances of the absence will be reviewed before determining whether corrective action is appropriate.”

Clara making the schedule doesn’t automatically make this her fault—or clear Mateo—but **when and how she communicated it matters**. Document the staffing impact separately, and make the discipline decision after checking those facts, rather than while you’re still covering the counter.

Right, that's fair—I need to check with Clara before I file anything. But I'm still stuck on the fact that Mateo saw the schedule Sunday and said nothing until 3:30 today. Four days of silence feels like he was hoping I'd just scramble.

Being left to cover both stations is frustrating, and it makes sense that the late notice feels personal right now. But **knowing about the shift Sunday isn’t the same as knowing Sunday that he couldn’t work it.** The four days of silence don’t establish that he expected you to scramble.

The question to ask Mateo is:
> “You saw the schedule Sunday and notified us at 3:30 Wednesday. When did you first know you wouldn’t be able to work the shift?”

If he knew about a conflict Sunday and waited, that supports a concern about delayed notice. If something unexpected happened Wednesday, that’s a different situation.

Check the scheduling details with Clara, then give Mateo a chance to explain. For tonight, document the notification time and the coverage impact—leave his presumed motive out of the record.
You're right that I don't know when he actually knew he couldn't work it. I'll give him a chance to explain before I file anything.

That sounds like a fair next step. You can still address the short notice and its impact—just let his explanation inform whether a write-up is warranted.

For tonight, jot down the facts while they’re fresh and leave the decision until after you’ve spoken with Clara and Mateo. Being frustrated doesn’t mean you can’t handle it fairly.
I hear you. I'll document the facts tonight and talk to Mateo tomorrow before deciding anything. Thanks for talking me down from filing while I was hot.
You’re welcome. You can be frustrated about covering both stations and still give Mateo a fair hearing. You’ve got a solid plan for tomorrow—I hope the rest of tonight eases up.
Alright. I'll document the facts tonight and talk to Mateo tomorrow before deciding anything. Thanks for helping me step back.
You’re welcome. Leave the decision for tomorrow—tonight, just capture the facts and get through your shift. Hope the rest of it is quieter.
